extraction_notes: Source: Quarry Valley (QV) district Program of Studies, 24 pages (catalogs/proctor-junior-senior-high-school/catalog_undated.pdf; folder is Proctor's, used per instruction because it covers Poultney, Proctor and West Rutland), text generated with `extract_text.py poultney-high-school <that pdf>` (page numbers = PAGE markers in phase2/text/poultney-high-school.txt). The PDF is undated and carries no year; internal evidence (QV graduation requirements 'Current' and 'For Class of 2027 and Beyond', principals listed, 2026-27 handbook uses same tables) suggests ~2025-27, so catalog_school_year is 'unknown'. This supersedes the earlier extraction built from the 2022-23 Poultney Program of Studies. Selection: kept every entry whose school tag includes PoHS (incl. 'WRS, PrHS, PoHS', 'WRS & PoHS', 'PrHS, PoHS', 'PoHS, and PrHS', 'WRS, PoHS') and untagged entries (offering_note 'district catalog - school not specified'): Survival Literature, a second 'Modern U.S. History' (page 8, differs from the PoHS-tagged 'Modern US History'), Lifetime Fitness (.5), Fitness and Nutrition (.5). Excluded as tagged for other schools only (WRS/PrHS), including 'Sports & Society (WRH)' (tag WRH is not a Poultney tag; presumably West Rutland). The Science of Science Fiction I & II and Spanish III & IV share one heading/description and are split into two records each. Credits and 'Prerequisite' text copied as stated; prerequisites also left inside the verbatim description. length is 'unknown' unless the entry says semester/quarter (Piano 1, Piano 2, Personal Fitness, Fitness and Nutrition (.5), 2-D Art, 3-D Art = semester; Career Exploration = quarter); grade_levels only stated for Intro to STEM. The catalog has no course codes, no CTE-center program list (Stafford Technical Center is only mentioned in Foundations of Math), no online courses and no separate dual-enrollment/early-college program entries, so no such records. Comparison with the 2022-23 Poultney catalog (catalogs/poultney-high-school/catalog_2022-23.pdf), titles that no longer appear for Poultney in the QV catalog: Film Analysis; Comparative Religion; Algebra 1A and Algebra 1B; Forensic Anatomy and Physiology; Intro to STEM II (now a single Intro to STEM); Kitchen Chem; Weather & Climate; Astronomy (now PrHS only); French I and French II; Guitar I; Music in Film; Online Courses; Dual Enrollment (general program); Intro to College Studies; Early College Program;. Old numbered titles English 9-12, Civics 9, Global Studies 10, U.S History 11, Integrated Mathematics 1-4, Advanced 2-D/3-D Art and Pre-Calculus Part I/II appear under different or revised titles (Literature and Composition, World Literature, American Literature, British Literature; Civics, Global Studies, U.S. History; Integrated Math I-IV; 2-D Art/3-D Art; Pre-Calculus I/II); the catalog does not say which old course maps to which new one, so no mapping is asserted. New since 2022-23: British Literature, Survival Literature, Foundations of English, Practical Chemistry, Lifetime Fitness, Fitness and Nutrition, Personal Finance, Career Exploration and Post Secondary Planning, Chorus/Band as 0.5 credits per semester. Graduation requirements: taken from the QV Student/Family Handbook 2026-27 (catalogs/west-rutland-school/grad_requirements_2026-27_QV_handbook.pdf, PDF pages 9-10; source_page 9), which applies district-wide, not from the program of studies. The program of studies page 2 states the same 28-credit structure in two tables (Current without a world-language credit, 27 credits for STC students; Class of 2027 and Beyond with 1.0 World Language/World Culture) - the handbook's table includes the world-language credit. The handbook file is not in source_files because that list is restricted to this school's folder; it is cited here.

courses.description: Students will be introduced to high school level proficiencies through direct instruction of texts, literary terms, and structures (both nonfiction and fiction). This course also stresses the continued improvement of writing skills with special emphasis on organization and development. This course focuses on the review of the fundamentals of grammar and usage as well as introducing a variety of literary genres such as: the short story, poetry, drama and the novel. The course is designed to teach the process skills of reading comprehension and the writing process.
courses.notes: School tag in catalog: WRS, PrHS, PoHS

courses.description: Students will read diverse literature from around the world in a variety of mediums including novels, poetry, drama, short stories, non-fiction, and graphic novels. This course will focus on developing both written and oral communication skills to prepare students to engage in fluent and responsible communication and to analyze information that comes to them in many forms of expression.
courses.notes: School tag in catalog: WRS, PrHS, PoHS

courses.description: American Literature will focus on critical analysis, which focuses on the standards and grade level expectations, with writing assignments designed for the students to continue their development as discriminating learners. There will be an emphasis placed on research of both primary and secondary documents. This course will include novels, plays, poems, and short stories. Writing will reflect the themes present in these works, and class discussion will revolve around thinking deeply about who we are as Americans and as individuals.
courses.notes: School tag in catalog: WRS, PrHS, PoHS

courses.description: This course explores primarily British literary types and themes. The course continues with the basic principles of critical writing. Included are literature based essays and analytical investigations designed to improve students’ literary perception and writing styles. College level work is developed.
courses.notes: School tag in catalog: PoHS

courses.description: Public Speaking is designed to provide students with an abundance of opportunities to speak, in a variety of forms, in front of audiences of people. Students will read and study both vocal and body techniques that contribute to effective presentations. Reading, research, note taking and speech writing are emphasized; as well, students will explore dramatic kinds of speaking such as monologues, dialogues and other theatrical performances. The focus of the course is to provide students with opportunities to speak often and in return receive both peer and teacher feedback in an effort to help develop poised communicators.
courses.notes: School tag in catalog: PoHS, and PrHS

courses.description: In this course, students will develop basic competencies and functional skills in the areas of listening, speaking, reading and writing. Instruction is interactive and multi-sensory. Attention is given to developing decoding and encoding skills in reading and written language, as well as reading comprehension using literature, newspapers and other high-interest low-level reading materials. Recommendation of teacher(s) is required.
courses.notes: School tag in catalog: WRS & PoHS; Foundations-level course; teacher recommendation required

courses.description: What inspires us to endure in the face of devastating and seemingly insurmountable obstacles? From survival of the human spirit to survival of the species, this course will explore fiction, non-fiction, poetry, and film to analyze and discuss the true meaning of survival. Through individual inquiry and group discussion, students will examine the writer's craft and historical context to determine the theme and purpose of each piece.
courses.notes: No school tag in catalog

courses.description: Civics will examine what it means to be an American. Students will learn about the foundations of the American political system, and what values and principles are basic to American constitutional democracy. Students will learn about the relationship we as citizens have with our government and will examine the rights and responsibilities of citizens. The course also examines the structure of the U.S. government and how it functions.
courses.notes: School tag in catalog: WRS, PrHS, PoHS

courses.description: Global Studies will examine world history, world cultures, and international relations from the 1400s into modern times. Emphasis will be placed on current events as they relate to historical events. This course is designed to give students opportunities to learn about our increasingly interdependent world.
courses.notes: School tag in catalog: WRS, PrHS, PoHS

courses.description: U.S. History is a survey of US history from the Civil War era to modern times. Topics may include industrialization, immigration, globalization, war and peace, civil rights and significant political, socioeconomic, and cultural developments in the U.S. since the Civil War.
courses.notes: School tag in catalog: WRS, PrHS, PoHS

courses.description: Modern U.S. History will examine U.S. history since 1945. This class will discuss post World War II American society and culture, the Cold War, expanding U.S. foreign relations, Korean War, Vietnam, the social/political movements of the 1960s, America’s involvement in the Middle East, the divide between liberalism and conservatism, and the evolution of modern American culture.
courses.notes: School tag in catalog: PoHS; Another untagged "Modern U.S. History" entry also appears on page 8

courses.description: Intro to Psychology is designed to help students understand the varied topic of psychology. This course will introduce topics such as learning, memory, sensation, perception, personality development, behavior, and abnormal psychology. Historical and contemporary research techniques as well as important historical figures in the field of psychology will also be a focus.
courses.notes: School tag in catalog: PrHS, PoHS

courses.description: Modern U.S. History explores the key events and cultural shifts in the United States since 1945. This engaging class examines post-World War II society, the Cold War, U.S. foreign relations, the Korean and Vietnam Wars, the impactful social and political movements of the 1960s, and America's involvement in the Middle East. We will also discuss the ongoing divide between liberalism and conservatism and the evolution of contemporary American culture. Join us to uncover the compelling stories that have shaped modern America.
courses.notes: No school tag in catalog; Second, separate "Modern U.S. History" entry (different description) from the PoHS-tagged "Modern US History"

courses.description: Algebra 1 begins with a basic review of order of operations, ratios, and proportions leading into the topic of Observed and Theoretical Probability. Students will study the different forms of linear equations, intercept form, standard form, and point-slope form and apply the various forms to real world applications. Students will study systems of linear equations and systems of inequalities with the focus on graphing, substitution and elimination methods with an introduction to matrices. Students will study exponents and exponential equations involving exponential growth and decay. Students will study rational functions; linear, exponential, and quadratic. The focus toward the end of the course will be working with polynomials, multiplying and factoring, the zero product property, and roots of quadratic equations.
courses.notes: School tag in catalog: WRS, PrHS, PoHS

courses.description: A study of Mathematics that begins with undefined and defined terms. Students use the undefined and defined terms throughout the course to build a basic understanding of mathematical systems. Students study the topics of inductive and deductive reasoning, congruence of polygons, similarity of geometric figures, properties of circles, area of regular and complex geometric figures as well as the volume of geometric solids. Students explore the geometric concepts throughout the course using classical construction tools, the compass and straightedge. Students will also use their knowledge of Algebra to study aspects of coordinate geometry, the Pythagorean Theorem, and introductory trigonometry.
courses.notes: School tag in catalog: WRS, PrHS, PoHS

courses.description: In this course students’ understanding of prior algebra skills and concepts will be extended to include topics essential to a second year course. Topics include recursion, data analysis, linear systems, functions, transformations, exponents and logarithms, polynomial functions, conic sections, rational functions, and trigonometry. Graphing calculators and appropriate technology will be used to enhance understanding and extend exploration in many areas. This course is open to all students who have successfully completed proficiencies in Algebra I and Geometry.
courses.notes: School tag in catalog: WRS, PrHS, PoHS

courses.description: This course is a study of the functions used in calculus, including linear, quadratic, polynomial, rational, inverse, exponential, logarithmic and trigonometric functions. In addition, students will study arithmetic and geometric sequences. Significant use of a graphing calculator will be expected. Prerequisite: Successful completion of Algebra 2 and recommendation of teacher.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Algebra 2 and recommendation of teacher.
courses.notes: School tag in catalog: PoHS

courses.description: This course may include the following topics of study: vector operations and problem solving, matrix operations and problem solving, sequences and series, trigonometric identities, Law of Sines, Law of Cosines, conic sections, and probability. These topics are used in calculus as well as many other higher level math courses. Course topics may be selected based on the interests and needs of the course participants. Significant use of a graphing calculator will be expected.
courses.notes: School tag in catalog: PoHS; Description continues across a page break

courses.description: AP Calculus AB is designed to be the equivalent of a first semester college calculus course devoted to topics in differential and integral calculus. The course focuses on students’ understanding of calculus concepts and provides experience with methods and applications. Students are required to use definitions and theorems to build arguments and justify conclusions. The course features a multi-representational approach to calculus, with concepts, results, and problems expressed graphically, numerically, analytically, and verbally. Exploring connections among these representations builds understanding of how calculus applies limits to develop important ideas, definitions, formulas, and theorems. A sustained emphasis on clear communication of methods, reasoning, justifications, and conclusions is essential. Teachers and students should regularly use technology to reinforce relationships among functions, to confirm written work, to implement experimentation, and to assist in interpreting results. This course prepares students to take the College Board’s exam in May.
courses.notes: School tag in catalog: PoHS

courses.description: This dual enrollment course is an introduction to the basic ideas and techniques of probability and statistics. Topics may include numerical and graphical descriptive measures, probability, random variables, the normal distribution, sampling theory, estimation, hypothesis testing, correlation, and regression. The use of technology may be required. Students must take a math assessment for placement purposes prior to registration. Prerequisite: Math & Algebra for College or equivalent skills. Prerequisite: Students must have completed Algebra II.
courses.prerequisites: Math & Algebra for College or equivalent skills. Prerequisite: Students must have completed Algebra II.
courses.notes: School tag in catalog: WRS, PoHS; Dual enrollment (CCV)

courses.description: This course is a study of the functions used in calculus, including the exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric functions.
courses.notes: School tag in catalog: PoHS; Dual enrollment (CCV)

courses.description: The foundations level course is for students who need to develop basic and functional life skills, or career specific skills in math. These are students who will benefit from small group or individual lessons and a hands-on approach to learning. This course is designed for those students requiring instruction in basic knowledge of math for everyday living,during and after high school, as well as those needing to master basic skills. Units will vary yearly depending on the needs of the students in the class. Examples of units include, financial math: banking, employment, budgeting, consumer skills, credit and debit; basic operations related to daily living skills: cooking, cleaning and shopping ; specific career paths for future jobs or acceptance at Stafford Technical Center; basic computation and fractions;and other topics related to specific needs of individual students. This course may be taken for multiple years for credit, with different topics each semester. Recommendation of teacher(s) is required.
courses.notes: School tag in catalog: PoHS; Description continues across a page break; Foundations-level course; teacher recommendation required

courses.description: Integrated I reviews math concepts taught in middle school math as well as introducing students to algebraic concepts of study. Topics include solving linear and absolute value equations, rewriting algebraic formulas and solving simple and compound inequalities. Additional topics of study are functions and function notation, graphing linear and absolute value equations and writing equations for linear functions. The course concludes with a study of lines of best fit, linear regression and arithmetic sequences.
courses.notes: School tag in catalog: PoHS

courses.description: This course includes instruction on Algebra, Geometry and Statistics. This course requires students to participate in investigations leading to: inequalities and linear programming, matrix operations, Pythagorean Theorem and right triangle trigonometry, probability, volume and surface areas. the study of geometry through right triangle trigonometry, volume and surface area, and transformational geometry; the retaining emphasis on the presentation and interpretation of data, through the study of measures of central tendency, apportionment, and sampling; and the introduction of exponential laws and models, function transformations, limits of sequences and matrices. The course will also review the basic skill of arithmetic, number properties, and basic geometric concepts of two-dimensional geometry. Students will further their understanding of mathematical concepts through investigations and discussions that apply and use mathematics. Prerequisite: Successful completion of Integrated Math I.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Integrated Math I.
courses.notes: School tag in catalog: PoHS

courses.description: Integrated III begins with a study of solving systems of linear equations and linear inequalities. Properties of exponents, exponential functions and geometric sequences are studied next. In addition, students study operations with polynomial functions as well as factoring and solving polynomial equations. The course concludes with a unit on graphing quadratic functions. Students should expect significant use of a graphing calculator in this course. Prerequisite: Successful completion of Integrated Math I and II.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Integrated Math I and II.
courses.notes: School tag in catalog: PoHS

courses.description: This course includes instruction on Algebra, Geometry and Statistics. This course requires students to participate in investigations leading to: three dimensional coordinate systems; trigonometric ratios in general triangles; combinatorics; linear and quadratic functions; modeling data; and mathematics of finance. The course will also review basic skills of arithmetic, number properties, and basic geometric concepts of two-dimensional geometry. Students will further their understanding of mathematical concepts through investigations and discussions that apply and use mathematics. Prerequisite: Successful completion of Integrated Math I-III.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Integrated Math I-III.
courses.notes: School tag in catalog: PoHS

courses.description: Earth Science is the first high school course in science. Earth Science is the study of the world around you. In this course, students will study earth, both as it exists by itself, and as part of the solar system. Topics and themes include the structure of the earth, astronomy, the atmosphere, weather, climate, geology, and the impacts humans have on the planet. Students may choose to work towards earning Honors, with increased expectations.
courses.notes: School tag in catalog: WRS, PrHS, PoHS; Honors option: "Students may choose to work towards earning Honors, with increased expectations."

courses.description: Biology is the scientific study of living organisms. Students participating in this course will develop an understanding of the principles of biology including, lab safety, scientific processes, ecology, cells, genetics, evolution and the six kingdoms. The course considers the interactions among the vast number of organisms that inhabit planet Earth. It presents the basic form and function of these organisms, from cells to organ systems, and simple to complex cellular structure. It delves into interactions between organisms, and between an organism and its environment. Laboratory work, hands-on activities and some dissections will help students on their journey through the amazing living world. Students may choose to work towards earning Honors, with increased expectations.
courses.notes: School tag in catalog: WRS, PrHS, PoHS; Honors option: "Students may choose to work towards earning Honors, with increased expectations."

courses.description: Chemistry is the study of the composition and properties of substances, and the changes that such substances can undergo. Students will explore the fundamental principles of chemistry which characterize the properties of matter and how it reacts. Topics may include, but are not limited to: measurement, atomic structure, electron configuration, the periodic table bonding, gas laws, properties of liquids and solids, solutions, stoichiometry, reactions, kinetics, equilibrium, and acids and bases. Students may choose to work towards earning Honors, with increased expectations. To be successful at the Honors level work, students should have strong algebra and proportional reasoning skills. Prerequisite: Students must have completed Earth Science, Algebra I and Geometry or instructor permission.
courses.prerequisites: Students must have completed Earth Science, Algebra I and Geometry or instructor permission.
courses.notes: School tag in catalog: WRS, PrHS, PoHS; Honors option: "Students may choose to work towards earning Honors, with increased expectations."

courses.description: Forensic Science I is designed to introduce students to key concepts and methods of forensic science, more commonly known as crime-scene investigation. To be successful in this course, students should be working toward meeting proficiency in Biology. Forensic Science is designed to introduce students to key concepts and methods of forensic science, more commonly known as crime-scene investigation. This course will include the following units of study: observation skills, evidence collection, death, fingerprints, DNA fingerprinting, blood and blood spatter, hair, fibers and textiles, pollen and spores, toxicology, handwriting analysis, soil, glass, forensic anthropology, casts and impressions, tool marks, and ballistics. This is a fast-paced hands-on course with frequent laboratory exercises embedded into class time. Prerequisite: Students must have completed or be enrolled in Biology.
courses.prerequisites: Students must have completed or be enrolled in Biology.
courses.notes: School tag in catalog: WRS, PrHS, PoHS

courses.description: Chemistry is the study of the composition and properties of substances, and the changes that such substances can undergo. Students will explore the basic principles of chemistry which characterize the properties of matter and how it reacts. Like all sciences, the science of chemistry is an organized and systematic attempt to understand the world around us. Through many activities students will explore the world of chemistry and see how it is applicable in laboratory situations. All students will develop good methods of problem solving and proper laboratory technique. Topics include, but are not limited to: measurement, atomic structure, electron configuration, the periodic table, properties of liquids and solids, solutions, reactions, equilibrium, and acids and bases.
courses.notes: School tag in catalog: PoHS

courses.description: This course will focus on basic physics concepts including forces and interactions, energy, and waves, electricity, and electromagnetism along with crosscutting concepts from various science courses. Concepts will be related to the world around us through discussion, labs, and projects. This course will rely heavily on project based learning, such as egg drop, bridge building, clean energy design, rollercoaster, and mouse trap cars. Strong emphasis is placed on in-person lab participation. This course alternates on odd years. Recommended for 10th grade and up.

courses.description: These half credit courses will investigate the history of science fiction films as well as the real science that inspires these great cinematic adventures. This course is focused on project based learning through the lens of science topics in life and physical science. Students can take section I, section II, or both for credit. Strong emphasis is placed on in-person lab participation.

courses.description: Marine biology is the study of organisms in the ocean and the physical and chemical properties of the ocean that influence underwater life. This is an introductory course with many hands-on activities. Topics of study include the seafloor, seawater and the world ocean, basics of biology, marine life, and marine ecosystems.
courses.notes: School tag in catalog: PrHS, PoHS

courses.description: Students in physical education classes follow a structured curriculum focusing on two areas: individual/team sports and introduction to fitness. The individual/team sports curriculum includes a variety of activities designed to enhance self-confidence, group dynamics, and coordination and movement skills. The introduction to fitness curriculum focuses on the five components of fitness, instructing students in the basics of exercise physiology and providing insight into the importance of life-time activities. Students are assessed on their ability to successfully complete required activities and class projects. Teachers use a grading rubric to help students understand expectations and track performance. As in all physical education classes, each student will be evaluated on participation, attitude, projects and/or written tests.
courses.notes: School tag in catalog: WRS, PrHS, PoHS

courses.description: 3 standards the whole class will be based around: 1.Selects and participates in physical activities (e.g., dance, yoga, aerobics) that meet the need for self-expression. 2.Applies knowledge of movement sequences to create or participate in one or more forms of dance. 3.Demonstrates appropriate technique in flexibility training. In this class we will practice mobility routines to increase our flexibility. Self expression will be explored by researching dance genres, choreographing short dances, practicing several yoga methods, engaging in pilates and imagery. Come try these lifetime fitness activities so you can grow your knowledge and tap into the benefits of each.
courses.notes: No school tag in catalog

courses.description: Students learn about the health related fitness components, healthy lifestyles, nutrition and other aspects of health and wellness. This physical education class performs various types of workouts three days a week. Students will learn to self-monitor through reflections, self-assessing and producing a wellness portfolio. Students will develop a fitness and nutrition plan and have the semester to try to work towards and achieve these goals. The goal of this course is to allow students to investigate topics around fitness and wellness in today's society while being able to work towards current health goals.
courses.notes: No school tag in catalog

courses.description: Personal fitness is based completely on each individual student's goals. It covers numerous topics throughout the semester, focusing on the Five Components of Fitness. Once individual goals are created the student will research the best types of exercises to perform. Nutrition will also be discussed. The overall goal for this course is to teach students to create their own workout plans, eat healthier, and be prepared to continue exercising on their own after the course and after they graduate high school.
courses.notes: School tag in catalog: PoHS

courses.description: To build students' health knowledge and skills development in an effort to prepare and empower students to value and engage in healthy lifestyles. The course content includes: body structure, human growth and development, family and mental health, nutrition, prevention of disease, safety, personal health habits, drugs and alcohol. The skills that will be developed in this class are: decision making, communication skills, examination of values and attitudes, location and evaluation of health related information, application and coping skills.
courses.notes: School tag in catalog: WRS, PrHS, PoHS; Catalog also lists a PrHS-only 0.5 credit "Health"; not included

courses.description: This course will cover the basics of art with a developing understanding of the elements and principles of design. Students will learn a variety of 2-dimensional techniques using pencils, pastels, watercolor, acrylics, printmaking, and collage. They will also discover 3-dimensional techniques through papier mache, clay, paper, and wood. Homework will be due weekly and will cover artists and/or cultures related to the project being created. In addition students will learn how to build their own professional art portfolio and utilize Google tools. This course is a prerequisite to upper level art classes.
courses.notes: School tag in catalog: PoHS; Description continues across a page break

courses.description: This class will take pencils and paint to a whole new level. Students will develop advanced techniques with pencils, pastels, watercolor, acrylics, and oils. They will create realistic, abstract, and non-representational work. Would you like to have more than one piece of your art to share? Do you yearn to try new and unusual materials? Students will develop advanced techniques in printmaking through linoleum and wood block, as well as etchings, and monotypes. Homework will be due weekly and will cover artists and/or cultures related to the project being created. In addition students will learn how to build their own professional art portfolio, take part in class critiques, and utilize Google tools. Students will spend the last part of the semester in an independent studio to gain proficiency in a chosen media. Ths course alternates every odd year. Prerequisite: Foundations of Art
courses.notes: School tag in catalog: PoHS

Students will learn about sculpture, architecture, and ceramics as they use paper, clay, papier mache, and wood. Homework will be due weekly and will cover artists and/or cultures related to the project being created. In addition students will learn how to build their own professional art portfolio, take part in class critiques, and utilize Google tools. Students will spend the last part of the semester in an independent studio to gain proficiency in a chosen 3-dimensional media. Ths course alternates every odd year. Prerequisite: Foundations of Art

They will construct pieces using coiling and slab techniques as well as becoming proficient on electric and kick pottery wheels. Students will learn how to pour and use molds. Students will observe how pottery has been used by a variety of cultures and understand how it has evolved over time. In addition students will learn how to build their own professional art portfolio and utilize Google tools. Prerequisite: Foundations of Art

courses.description: Let’s take pixels to a whole new level. This course merges art with advertising and has students working with clients. Students will master photo and film manipulation using both PCs and Macs. A variety of equipment and techniques will be explored to enhance photography and film. They will create a relationship with a business, develop a budget, create a business plan, and negotiate sales. Students will also discover their voice as a visual artist and present their art to a worldwide audience. Prerequisite: Foundations of Art
courses.notes: School tag in catalog: PoHS

courses.description: Let’s punch up the pixels and further the films... This course expands on Digital Arts and puts students in a leadership role within the class. They will continue to work with MACs and PCs and develop advanced techniques in photography and film as they work in an expanded independent studio on their own projects. They do promotional work for the high school and the district as well as helping out a business of their choice. Homework will be due weekly and will cover artists and/or cultures related to the project being created. In addition students will learn how to build their own professional art portfolio, take part in class critiques, and utilize Google tools. Prerequisite: Digital Arts I

courses.description: This dual enrollment course requires students to explore the mechanical and electronic aspects of digital photography as well as the basic tools of image manipulation. The course also includes the study of design, composition, and aesthetics of digital images. Access to a digital camera and some previous photography experience are required.

courses.description: This class develops and refines the basics of choral singing. Tone quality, breath support, sound production, rhythm reading, and harmony are explored. Music listening, improvising and composing are also included in the curriculum. Once a week, students are required to attend a small-group/individual lesson where group/individualized instruction is given to work on choral music. Extra lessons will be available for students who choose to participate in festivals or other performance audition groups. Chorus performances include the Poultney High School Winter and Spring Concerts and performance field trips which all chorus students are required to attend. No prior musical experience is necessary to be in chorus, and everyone is welcome.

courses.description: This course is a performance-based class where the basic skills of instrument playing are taught and refined. Listening, improvising, and self and group reflection are included in the curriculum. Once a week, students are required to attend a small-group/individual lesson where group/individualized instruction is given to work on band music. Extra lessons will be available for students who choose to participate in festivals, other performance audition groups or who want to challenge themselves beyond the band music. Students progress at their own speed according to their experience level upon entering the class. Beginners as well as more advanced students are welcome. The Poultney High School Band performs at area parades, winter and spring concerts, and other performance field trips which all band students are all required to attend.

courses.description: This is an introductory course in the fundamentals of piano keyboard performance. Classroom topics include the study of musical notation and symbols, the performance of simple melodies, standard scales and chord progressions, folk songs, and popular music. Students will have public and class performances throughout the semester. Performances include classroom performances, a midterm performance and a final recital performance.
courses.notes: School tag in catalog: PoHS

courses.description: The Intermediate Piano course is offered as a continuation of the Piano 1: Basic Piano course. Materials and content are taught at a higher level of difficulty. An emphasis will be placed on the study of piano literature within each period of music history (Baroque, Classical, Romantic, and 20th Century). All students in the Intermediate Piano Keyboard course will build upon the skills attained in the Piano 1: Basic Piano course. Some student compositions will also be included. Students will have public and class performances throughout the semester. Performances include classroom performances, a midterm performance and a final recital performance. Prerequisites: Prior success at reading treble/bass clef and rhythmic notation and/or completion of the Piano 1 or a class equivalent to basic theory or basic piano.

courses.description: Students enrolled in this course will look at the question, “why is music taught in school?” from a variety of angles and through different lenses. Units include looking at famous musicians from a multiple of genres throughout time, music composition using either Garageband and/or traditional music notation, music and the brain (how music affects our emotions), music and movement, musician political voice, and more.

courses.description: Students will learn to understand spoken Spanish using vocabulary and constructions appropriate for the earliest phases of language learning. Students work toward proficiency in listening, speaking, reading, writing, and cultural competency. Students will be able to answer questions, and ask these questions in the appropriate situations. Students will follow and carry on basic conversations using familiar construction and vocabulary. Students will read and write all material learned orally. Countries in which Spanish is spoken will be culturally explored.

Students will develop practical skills to manage their personal finances while applying them to real-life applications. These skills will provide students a solid foundation that will guide them in making informed decisions, promote financial independence, ensure personal security, and work towards maintaining a stable financial future. courses.description: Student enrollment in Driver’s Education is limited to 20 students per class, and selection will be prioritized by student’s date of birth. A student must have a valid Vermont Learner’s permit on the first day of class. A proficiency grade will be issued for driver’s education. This course consists of five parts: ● Classroom component (at least 30 hours) which may be conducted in-person or remotely. ● Behind the wheel component (at least 6 hours), The B-T-W and observation time is done in the Driver education vehicle. ● Observation component (at least 6 hours) ● Parent/Guardian component (practice driving time). Parent component is 40 hours of supervised practice driving time of which 25 hours is during student enrollment in the Driver Education Course. ● Social Responsibility component (student’s attitudes and behaviors). Students are expected to follow appropriate GRCSU Health and Safety Guidelines, demonstrate self-respect to themselves and others, think before they act, accept responsibility for their actions, participate in group discussions and follow the rules in the school setting and outside on the road. If minimum attendance requirements are not met, the student will be dropped from the course. How is a student assessed? (Learning Target/Course Assessments) ● In the classroom phase, the student must score at least proficient on each unit discussed, and score at least 80 on the final exam. ● Students must show they are responsible citizens with socially responsible attitudes and behaviors. Attitudes and behaviors will have a bearing on whether students will receive a Driver Education Completion Certificate. ● In the driving phase, the student will have a driving route to practice various techniques and skills. ● Students will be given a mock final road test for their final drive. They must score at least 80% proficiency on the Driver Education Final Road Test. ● Parents will be required to attend a parent meeting or schedule an initial check-in meeting with the instructor. What will Driver Education students learn? (Enduring Understanding/Indicators) The classroom has nine units of knowledge and understanding. It includes but is not limited to the following: Getting ready to drive, understanding driver vehicle readiness, laws of the road, basic driving, maneuvers (parallel park, VT Turnaround, and hill start), managing risks, time and space, rural and city driving, interstate driving, impaired driving, distracted driving, use of the safety systems, physics and car crashes, biology and car crashes, adverse conditions, environmental issues, insurance, basic car and tire maintenance, and trip planning.

courses.course_name: Career Exploration and Post Secondary Planning
courses.description: This course is the second half of Drivers Ed. In Career Exploration, students will take a look at various post secondary opportunities, career options and how their personal interests, aptitudes, and values fit into the overall picture of choosing a fitting career. The students will have an opportunity to see different college and career paths, and talk to speakers to gain a better understanding as to how they can take their education and transition into a career opportunity. Students will also take a look at goal-setting and the decision making process in order to better understand how decisions we make today can affect our futures. During this quarter course students will: ● Explore post secondary planning, careers, and paths that will lead them to make the right choices towards their future ● Have the opportunity to talk to professionals both in and outside of the classroom ● Take field trips to enhance their understand of different post secondary opportunities, college, careers, and professions ● Complete a research project based on one career of interest Students will demonstrate their understanding of different careers during a community based presentation at the end of the quarter where they will present their findings to the elementary school.
